expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Applying the AAIDD Supports Paradigm Over IQ-Only Ceilings
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A 15-year-old ninth grader with moderate intellectual disability (FSIQ 56) enjoys robotics club, reads community signage, and needs intermittent prompting for budgeting. Staff give the student cartoon toddler stickers as reinforcers, cite the IQ score as a learning ceiling, and propose permanent self-contained placement.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Use the AAIDD supports-intensity paradigm with age-respectful materials, inclusive electives, and tailored conceptual, social, and practical supports.
expandableCase.explanation: AAIDD defines intellectual functioning through the interaction of individual strengths, environment, and personalized supports rather than a static IQ ceiling. Infantilizing adolescents with preschool rewards and defaulting to segregation undermine dignity, LRE mandates, and adaptive skill growth.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In reviewing early developmental evidence, a kindergarten teacher notices that one child reaches several language milestones later than classmates. What is the most appropriate first interpretation?
choices: Broad developmental patterns allow wide variation, so the team should gather multi-source data across settings before drawing conclusions.
Falling below the typical classroom average on language milestones establishes a developmental disability that warrants formal eligibility.
The team should assign a provisional disability label promptly so specialized speech-language interventions can begin before gathering family input.
Chronological age norms become uninformative once a child trails classmates, so expectations should be based on informal adult impressions instead.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Milestones provide useful reference points, not stand-alone diagnoses. Educators should document functioning across domains, contexts, and time and involve qualified team members before attributing a pattern to disability. chapterTakeaways: AAIDD defines intellectual disability by concurrent significant limits in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior (conceptual, social, practical) originating before age 22.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Preventing Diagnostic Overshadowing of Coexisting Health Needs
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A 10-year-old with Down syndrome and mild intellectual disability begins squinting at print, covering their ears during hallway transitions, refusing seated tasks, and coughing while drinking juice. Staff attribute the shift to "stubbornness from intellectual disability" without checking the IHP or requesting screenings.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Avoid diagnostic overshadowing by consulting the nurse, verifying seizure and feeding IHP protocols, and requesting vision, hearing, and medical checks.
expandableCase.explanation: Students with intellectual disabilities face higher rates of coexisting vision, hearing, dysphagia, thyroid, and seizure conditions that often surface as sudden behavioral changes. Explaining away acute sensory or swallowing signs as disability traits delays critical medical care and creates serious aspiration hazards.

Deliver uniform remedial instruction across all core academic subjects so the student receives consistent skill reinforcement.
Interpret the persistent academic bottleneck as evidence of broadly limited cognitive ability across every learning domain.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Specific learning disabilities can affect particular psychological processes and academic skills unevenly. expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Leading Person-Centered Transition Planning by Age Sixteen
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: At a 16-year-old's annual IEP meeting, staff present prewritten goals focused on sorting colored beads, postpone transition assessment until age 18, direct all questions exclusively to the parent while the student sits quietly, and assume automatic placement in a segregated sheltered workshop after graduation.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Conduct transition assessments now, coach the student to voice preferences via visuals or AAC, and align IEP goals with competitive employment.
expandableCase.explanation: IDEA mandates postsecondary transition planning no later than age 16 driven by student strengths, interests, and measurable community-participation goals. Proxy-only meetings, detached busywork goals, and sheltered-workshop defaults violate self-determination principles and WIOA competitive integrated employment priorities.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: While drafting baseline present-level evidence, which present-level statement best supports individualized planning?
choices: The student expresses reluctance during extended writing tasks and continues to need frequent encouragement from adults.
Evaluation records document a specific learning disability in written expression affecting classroom writing assignments.

expandableCase.title: Presuming Authorship and Honoring Nonverbal Refusal in Writing
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: During seventh-grade persuasive writing, a paraprofessional moves an adolescent's hand to copy a model paragraph verbatim, asks rapid-fire yes/no prompts with zero pause time, and pulls the paper back each time the student pushes it away and shakes their head.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Honor communicative refusal, extend wait time, and teach authentic writing using word prediction, speech-to-text, or choice banks.
expandableCase.explanation: Hand-over-hand tracing and copying-only assignments replace authentic student authorship with adult output and suppress self-advocacy. knowledgeChecks.prompt: A student uses AAC to choose a topic but an adult composes the entire message. Which change would make writing more student directed?

Postpone all authentic writing tasks until the student can type independently on a standard keyboard.
Provide generative AAC vocabulary so the student drafts and revises text with minimal prompts.
Have an adult compose a polished finished message and ask the student to nod approval before sending.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Writing instruction should preserve authorship, not merely produce an adult-created product. Accessible generation and revision choices reveal student intent while systematic support can be faded as competence grows.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Fading Prompts and Programming Generalization in Functional Math
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: An 11th grader with moderate ID scores 95% identifying plastic coins at a classroom table when given immediate verbal hints on every trial, yet freezes at a real grocery checkout, unable to locate the register subtotal or select enough bills independently.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Use a checkout task analysis with total-task chaining, constant time delay (0s to 4s), next-dollar strategy, and community-based instruction.
expandableCase.explanation: Pairing task analysis with systematic constant time delay prevents prompt dependence, while teaching across multiple authentic stores, cashiers, and price points builds true generalization. Isolated classroom drills with immediate verbal prompting create fragile skills that collapse in real community settings.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A student is planning a purchase with a fixed budget and can use a calculator but needs help deciding which items fit. What should instruction emphasize?
choices: Take away the calculator and require mental paper-and-pencil addition before allowing school-store purchases.
Have a staff member pick out the items that fit the budget and read the final register total aloud.
Assign isolated drills typing random prices into the calculator without connecting totals to buying choices.
Model a budget comparison strategy with a calculator or visual guide, practice choices, and fade prompts.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: The instructional target is mathematical reasoning within a meaningful routine, not denial of an appropriate tool. Authentic comparison, accessible representation, and prompt fading build agency and generalizable budget use.

Keep every daily schedule minute fixed permanently so the student never encounters a routine adjustment.
Continue matching printed digital clock flashcards at a desk until worksheet speed reaches mastery.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Time use involves relating clock information to duration, sequence, and action. Varied practice in real routines plus accessible cues supports transfer and reduces dependence on adult transition commands.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Preventing IQ-Cutoff and Language-Difference Eligibility Errors
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A bilingual third grader scores 69 on an English-only IQ test given without visual instructions. Relying exclusively on that score and one teacher's brief adaptive checklist—with no parent interview or home-language evaluation—the team proposes intellectual disability eligibility.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Complete a nondiscriminatory evaluation integrating multi-informant home and school adaptive scales with accessible, linguistically valid testing.
expandableCase.explanation: IDEA and AAIDD require concurrent deficits in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior documented across multiple settings—never an IQ-cutoff-only or single-rater decision—while ruling out limited English proficiency as the determinant factor. Inaccessible English testing confounds language difference with ID.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When selecting or administering assessment for a student with an intellectual disability, a vocabulary test is used to decide whether a student can solve multistep equations. What is the primary concern?
choices: Validity, because the scores do not support the intended construct interpretation and decision.
Reliability, because numerical test scores fluctuate whenever vocabulary or spelling tasks are short.
Administration efficiency, because brief screening tools take less time than full-length unit exams.
National norming, because classroom skill evaluations must compare learners against national peer samples.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Validity concerns whether evidence supports the interpretation and use of scores. A measure dominated by a different skill cannot justify a conclusion about the intended construct. For 5322 preparation, connect intellectual and adaptive evidence to individualized, age-respectful instruction; presume competence; integrate communication, functional, academic, social, self-determination, and transition goals; fade support toward agency; and monitor meaningful participation and generalization.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When selecting or administering assessment for a student with an intellectual disability, a progress measure gives very different scores on consecutive days even though instruction and performance appear stable. What quality is in question?
choices: Face validity, or whether the assessment directions appear relevant to students and families.
Reliability, or the consistency of measurement across occasions and scorers.

diagrams.title: Intellectual Disability Identification: Intellectual Functioning, Adaptive Behavior & Support-Intensity Model
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Synthesize AAIDD and IDEA criteria—connecting intellectual functioning, conceptual/social/practical adaptive behavior, developmental onset, and cultural-linguistic validity to an individualized support-intensity model rather than fixed deficit ceilings.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking intellectual functioning, conceptual/social/practical adaptive domains, developmental onset and cultural-linguistic validity, and individualized support-intensity planning.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right flow from intellectual functioning and conceptual/social/practical adaptive behavior through developmental onset and cultural-linguistic validity to support-intensity profiling and inclusive outcomes.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, comprehensive evaluation assesses intellectual functioning—reasoning, problem solving, planning, and learning from experience—using individually administered, psychometrically sound measures without ever relying on an IQ score alone. Second, teams evaluate significant limitations in adaptive behavior across conceptual (literacy, money, time), social (interpersonal skills, social judgment, rule-following), and practical (self-care, safety, daily living, work) domains across home and school contexts. Third, evaluators confirm onset during the developmental period while interpreting results through cultural, linguistic, sensory, motor, and instructional-opportunity lenses to avoid bias. Fourth, rather than assigning fixed deficit ceilings, teams profile the intensity of individualized supports needed (intermittent, limited, extensive, or pervasive) alongside personal strengths. Finally, aligning tailored IEP supports, assistive technology, and natural community resources enhances human functioning and inclusive participation, with support intensity reassessed as skills and environments evolve.

Adaptive Behavior (Conceptual, Social & Practical): Document significant limitations across conceptual, social, and practical everyday skills using multi-informant evidence from caregivers, educators, and direct observation.

Developmental Onset & Cultural-Linguistic Validity: Verify onset during the developmental period while accounting for community culture, home language, communication mode, sensory/motor differences, and equitable learning opportunities.

Individualized Support-Intensity Profile: Move from deficit ceilings to an ecological supports framework that matches strengths with intermittent, limited, extensive, or pervasive supports across life domains.

Enhanced Human Functioning & Inclusive Access: Deliver personalized IEP instruction, assistive technology, and natural community supports to expand autonomy and belonging, revisiting support intensity dynamically as growth occurs.

diagrams.title: Coexisting Sensory, Motor, Communication & Health Support Coordination
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Coordinate cognitive-processing profiles with OT, PT, SLP, and nursing input, accessible response-mode matching, fatigue-aware pacing, and multisensory concrete-to-abstract instruction while preventing diagnostic overshadowing and ensuring strict IHP safety adherence.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teams map cognitive-processing variability alongside coexisting sensory, motor, complex communication, and chronic health needs while actively preventing diagnostic overshadowing—never attributing physical pain, hearing loss, or vision barriers to intellectual disability alone. Second, educators coordinate OT, PT, SLP, and school-nurse input into unified Individualized Healthcare Plans (IHPs), seizure response protocols, and safe feeding procedures. Third, teams match accessible response modes (switches, eye-gaze, AAC, adapted grasp) and assess fatigue and pacing needs so sensory or motor barriers never block learning. Fourth, teachers deliver multisensory concrete-to-abstract instruction paired with memory retrieval scaffolds, distributed practice, and integrated communication-motor routines. Finally, teams monitor health adherence, stamina, and skill retention to refine pacing and multidisciplinary supports.

Accessible Response-Mode & Pacing Match: Eliminate sensory-access barriers, align motor and AAC response modes, and schedule fatigue-aware pacing across school routines.

diagrams.title: Person-Centered Secondary Transition, Self-Determination & Supported Employment Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Coordinate age-appropriate transition assessment and student voice with measurable postsecondary goals, self-determination and job-coaching instruction, interagency linkage, and least-restrictive supported decision-making.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right transition flow from age-appropriate transition assessment and student voice through measurable postsecondary goals, self-advocacy and job coaching, and interagency linkage to supported decision-making and ethical dignity.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, beginning no later than age 16 (or earlier under state policy), teams conduct ongoing age-appropriate transition assessments—such as interest inventories, situational workplace observations, and person-centered planning (MAPS/PATH)—anchored in the student’s own voice and preferences. Second, assessment results drive measurable postsecondary goals in education/training, competitive integrated employment, and independent living where appropriate, aligned with annual IEP goals, transition services, and a coherent course of study. Third, educators explicitly teach self-determination, goal setting, self-advocacy, disability disclosure, and student-led IEP participation alongside work-based learning and supported-employment job coaching. Fourth, with parent or adult-student consent, the team invites Vocational Rehabilitation, developmental disability services, and postsecondary disability offices to coordinate adult eligibility and bridge the shift from IDEA entitlement to ADA/Section 504 access. Finally, at least one year before the age of majority, teams address transfer of rights and inform families of least-restrictive guardianship alternatives—such as supported decision-making—upholding autonomy, dignity of risk, and annual plan renewal.

diagrams.title: AAC, Multimodal Communication & Functional Behavior Replacement Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect multimodal communication assessment and feature-matched low-, mid-, and high-tech AAC to Functional Communication Training (FCT) replacement skills, aided language input, and home-school partner training.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking communicative repertoire assessment, feature-matched AAC selection, function-based behavior replacement (FCT), aided language modeling, and cross-setting partner training.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right flow from assessing communicative repertoire and access needs through feature-matched low/mid/high-tech AAC, function-matched replacement communication (FCT), and aided language modeling to home-school partner training.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teams assess the learner’s full multimodal communicative repertoire—vocalizations, gestures, eye gaze, symbols, and speech—alongside motor, vision, hearing, and positioning needs, presuming competence without requiring cognitive prerequisites. Second, specialists feature-match low-, mid-, and high-tech AAC options (such as communication boards, core-vocabulary books, or speech-generating devices with direct selection or switch scanning) to the student’s linguistic and access profile. Third, when challenging behavior serves an unmet communicative purpose, the team uses Functional Behavior Assessment to teach a faster, lower-effort, functionally equivalent communicative replacement via Functional Communication Training (FCT). Fourth, adults and peers model target vocabulary directly on the AAC system (aided language input) across authentic interactions for requesting, protesting, commenting, and socializing. Finally, partner training equips teachers, paraprofessionals, peers, and families to keep AAC accessible across home and school, feeding emerging vocabulary needs back into ongoing system updates.

Aided Language Modeling & Natural Practice: Model core and fringe vocabulary directly on the student’s AAC system across daily routines, honoring communicative attempts for requesting, refusing, commenting, and connecting.

diagrams.title: Ecological Inventory, Community-Based Instruction (CBI) & Independent Living Progression
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply the ecological inventory and discrepancy-analysis process to deliver Community-Based Instruction (CBI) under natural cues, integrate safety and self-management scaffolds, and transition toward natural community supports.
diagrams.caption: An original study progression from ecological inventory and discrepancy analysis through Community-Based Instruction under natural cues, self-management scaffolds, and natural supports.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right progression from ecological inventory of real environments through discrepancy analysis, Community-Based Instruction with natural cues, and safety/self-management scaffolds to natural community supports.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, educators partner with the student and family to complete an ecological inventory of current and future domestic, community, recreation, and vocational environments, cataloging authentic routines and required skills. Second, a discrepancy analysis compares the student’s current performance to each step of the routine, distinguishing skills to teach directly from steps supported via adaptations, assistive technology, or dignified partial participation. Third, teams deliver Community-Based Instruction (CBI) directly in authentic settings—such as grocery stores, transit stops, clinics, and workplaces—paired with classroom simulation so real environmental cues govern behavior. Fourth, instruction embeds personal safety, money and time management, picture or mobile checklists, and video self-monitoring prompts that foster independent self-correction. Finally, teams monitor skill maintenance and intentionally fade adult proximity to natural supports—coworkers, store signage, mobile reminders, and community routines—while cycling new ecological environments into future planning.

diagrams.title: Functional Academics, Standards-Aligned Alternate Access & UDL Integration
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect age-appropriate grade-level core standards to prioritized functional life-skills bridges, concrete manipulatives and UDL scaffolds, inclusive general-education LRE participation, and accessible progress monitoring.

Second, the IEP team builds a prioritized functional and life-skills bridge—linking literacy, budgeting, time/measurement, and comprehension directly to real-world utility, individualized goals, and alternate achievement benchmarks where appropriate. Third, teachers design Universal Design for Learning (UDL) scaffolds, pairing concrete-representational-abstract (CRA) manipulatives, adapted texts, graphic organizers, visual supports, and assistive technology. Fourth, students participate actively in general-education classrooms in their Least Restrictive Environment (LRE) through co-teaching, peer supports, and targeted accommodations or modifications. First, the teacher performs a task analysis, breaking a complex academic, daily-living, or vocational routine into discrete, observable, sequential steps validated against real-world performance. Second, the team selects forward chaining, backward chaining, or total-task chaining based on the learner’s baseline mastery and need for immediate terminal reinforcement. Third, instruction delivers explicit modeling and systematic response prompting—such as constant time delay or a system of least prompts—paired with immediate behavior-specific praise and calm error correction. Fourth, step-by-step data guide systematic prompt fading and thinned reinforcement schedules to prevent prompt dependency and build fluent independence; if accuracy stalls, the instructor refines prompt timing or error correction. Finally, the team programs maintenance and generalization explicitly across varied materials, natural cues, people, and real-world settings.

Forward, Backward, or Total-Task Chaining: Choose forward chaining from step 1, backward chaining to give immediate contact with the natural end result, or total-task chaining when several steps are already mastered.

Systematic Prompting (Time Delay / Least Prompts): Apply explicit modeling with error-minimizing prompts—such as 0-second then 3–5-second constant time delay or system of least prompts—plus immediate reinforcement and error correction.
Data-Driven Prompt Fading: Graph independent vs. prompted steps and systematically reduce prompt intrusiveness to prevent prompt dependency, adjusting prompt level if performance plateaus.
Programmed Maintenance & Generalization: Teach across multiple exemplars, instructors, materials, and natural environmental cues so mastered chains endure and transfer reliably beyond training.

diagrams.title: Task-Analytic Progress Monitoring, FBA-to-BIP & AA-AAS Decision Loop
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect strict AA-AAS alternate-assessment eligibility safeguards, task-analytic prompt-level progress graphing, function-based FBA-to-BIP alignment, and implementation-fidelity audits to timely instructional revisions that prevent stagnation and punitive behavior plans.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, IEP teams apply strict state and federal eligibility criteria for Alternate Assessment based on Alternate Academic Achievement Standards (AA-AAS), reserving it strictly for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities aligned to grade-level essential elements and respecting overuse caps. Second, teachers graph task-analytic step mastery and prompt-level independence frequently to detect stagnation early. Third, when challenging behavior interferes with learning, teams conduct a Functional Behavioral Assessment (FBA) to identify behavioral function and align a positive Behavior Intervention Plan (BIP) teaching functionally equivalent communication replacements rather than relying on punitive consequences. Fourth, before changing student goals, teams audit adult implementation fidelity and analyze specific skill error patterns. Finally, educators execute data-driven instructional revisions and verify generalization across natural cues, feeding new performance data back into progress graphs.

Implementation-Fidelity & Error-Pattern Audit: Verify consistent adult delivery fidelity first, then diagnose step-level error patterns across settings.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, educators uphold IDEA Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE), Least Restrictive Environment (LRE), procedural safeguards, and FERPA/ADA confidentiality and access rights while preventing restrictive-procedure misuse and dignity breaches. Second, teams engage families as equal co-authors through culturally responsive conferencing, plain-language materials, and accessible home-school partnerships rather than excluding families from IEP drafting. Third, teachers embed self-determination rights education and dignity-of-risk learning choices so students practice informed decision-making safely across adolescence. Fourth, at least one year before the student reaches the age of majority, teams deliver formal transfer-of-rights notification and host family-centered transition workshops explaining adult legal options. Finally, educators inform families about less-restrictive guardianship alternatives—especially supported decision-making—countering automatic plenary-guardianship bias and protecting adult civil rights.

diagrams.title: Interdisciplinary Teaming, Paraprofessional Supervision & Evidence-Based Advocacy Cycle
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Coordinate interdisciplinary related services, ethical paraprofessional supervision and prompt-fading coaching, co-taught UDL planning, community-employer partnerships, and evidence-based professional learning without improper delegation or siloed pullout fragmentation.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow connecting role delineation and supervision standards, push-in therapy and UDL co-planning, paraeducator prompt-fading coaching, community-employer advocacy, and outcome-focused professional learning.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right flow from role delineation and supervision standards through push-in therapy and UDL co-planning, paraeducator prompt-fading coaching, and systemic community-employer advocacy to outcome-focused professional learning.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teams establish clear co-teaching and paraprofessional supervision standards so licensed special educators retain responsibility for primary instruction, assessment, and IEP decisions—preventing improper primary-instruction delegation and unsupervised medical-task risk. Second, special educators, general educators, and related-service therapists (OT, PT, SLP) design integrated push-in therapy schedules and collaborative UDL lessons instead of siloed pullout service fragmentation. Third, teachers provide structured paraeducator training, live modeling, and ongoing feedback focused on prompt fading and peer-interaction facilitation. Fourth, educators engage in systemic disability advocacy and build community-employer partnerships that expand authentic inclusive opportunities. Finally, teams conduct outcome-focused evaluations and pursue evidence-based professional learning to continuously replace outdated, non-evidence practices.

Push-In Related Services & Collaborative UDL: Integrate OT, PT, SLP, and co-teaching plans into shared inclusive schedules rather than siloed pullout fragmentation.
Paraeducator Training & Prompt-Fading Coaching: Deliver explicit plans, modeling, and constructive feedback so paraeducators fade prompts systematically and foster peer belonging.
Community-Employer Partnerships & Advocacy: Build local employer networks and practice systemic disability advocacy to expand inclusive school and adult-community participation.
Outcome Evaluation & Evidence-Based Learning: Review student outcome data collaboratively and engage in research-validated professional learning to retire outdated non-evidence practices.

diagramPlacements.learnerPurpose: Synthesize AAIDD and IDEA criteria—connecting intellectual functioning, conceptual/social/practical adaptive behavior, developmental onset, and cultural-linguistic validity to an individualized support-intensity model rather than fixed deficit ceilings.

Coordinate cognitive-processing profiles with OT, PT, SLP, and nursing input, accessible response-mode matching, fatigue-aware pacing, and multisensory concrete-to-abstract instruction while preventing diagnostic overshadowing and ensuring strict IHP safety adherence.

Coordinate age-appropriate transition assessment and student voice with measurable postsecondary goals, self-determination and job-coaching instruction, interagency linkage, and least-restrictive supported decision-making.

Connect multimodal communication assessment and feature-matched low-, mid-, and high-tech AAC to Functional Communication Training (FCT) replacement skills, aided language input, and home-school partner training.

Apply the ecological inventory and discrepancy-analysis process to deliver Community-Based Instruction (CBI) under natural cues, integrate safety and self-management scaffolds, and transition toward natural community supports.

Connect age-appropriate grade-level core standards to prioritized functional life-skills bridges, concrete manipulatives and UDL scaffolds, inclusive general-education LRE participation, and accessible progress monitoring.

Promote authentic authorship, pragmatic communication, and self-advocacy for students with intellectual disabilities by honoring communicative intent, selecting alternative pencils and speech-to-text tools, scaffolding composition with prompt fading, and avoiding hand-over-hand authorship replacement.

Design evidence-based systematic instruction for learners with intellectual disabilities by decomposing complex routines via task analysis, selecting forward/backward/total-task chaining, applying time delay or system of least prompts, fading prompts, and programming generalization.

Apply nondiscriminatory assessment validity, accommodations vs. modifications distinctions, multi-informant adaptive-behavior scales, developmental-period verification, and ecological curriculum-based baselines to make accurate AAIDD/IDEA eligibility and instructional decisions.

Connect strict AA-AAS alternate-assessment eligibility safeguards, task-analytic prompt-level progress graphing, function-based FBA-to-BIP alignment, and implementation-fidelity audits to timely instructional revisions that prevent stagnation and punitive behavior plans.

Integrate IDEA FAPE and LRE, FERPA and ADA protections, culturally responsive family conferencing, dignity-of-risk self-determination instruction, timely transfer-of-rights notification, and supported decision-making alternatives to automatic plenary guardianship.

Coordinate interdisciplinary related services, ethical paraprofessional supervision and prompt-fading coaching, co-taught UDL planning, community-employer partnerships, and evidence-based professional learning without improper delegation or siloed pullout fragmentation.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Prevent misidentification and diagnostic overshadowing in an ID referral
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate an incomplete Intellectual Disability eligibility referral for a multilingual fourth grader using AAIDD three-prong criteria and IDEA nondiscriminatory safeguards.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Marcus, a 9-year-old fourth grader with interrupted prior schooling and emerging English proficiency (WIDA Level 2), was referred for Intellectual Disability after scoring 68 on an English IQ test. A teacher-only adaptive scale yielded 71. Yet an interpreter-assisted parent interview revealed Marcus makes sibling snacks, runs errands safely, and translates notices. A nurse screen also flagged uncorrected myopia.
taskParts: Test the referral evidence against all three AAIDD criteria and explain why the current data cannot establish Intellectual Disability eligibility.
Analyze how limited English proficiency, interrupted schooling, and uncorrected myopia create diagnostic overshadowing and score invalidity.
Recommend a nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary re-evaluation and strengths-based supports plan before making any eligibility determination.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast the English FSIQ 68 and teacher-only adaptive 71 against Marcus's strong practical home-community functioning, WIDA Level 2 status, interrupted schooling, and uncorrected vision.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply AAIDD three-prong criteria and five operational assumptions alongside IDEA 34 CFR 300.304–300.306 nondiscriminatory testing and exclusionary factors (English proficiency and lack of instruction).

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Secure optometry follow-up and glasses, collect cross-setting conceptual-social-practical adaptive data with a bilingual evaluator, use nonverbal or home-language cognitive measures, and deliver explicit literacy-ELD scaffolds.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Document response to culturally responsive Tier 2 instruction, ensure interpreter-supported parental participation, and refrain from assigning an ID classification while exclusionary factors remain unaddressed.

successCriteria: Applies all three AAIDD criteria (intellectual functioning, adaptive behavior across conceptual-social-practical domains, developmental onset before age 22) plus AAIDD cultural-linguistic assumptions.
Identifies IDEA exclusionary rules prohibiting eligibility when limited English proficiency or lack of appropriate instruction is the determinant factor.
Flags uncorrected myopia and teacher-only adaptive sampling as critical validity threats causing diagnostic overshadowing.
Proposes vision correction, bilingual/nonverbal multimethod assessment, and immediate instructional supports rather than waiting passively.
commonPitfalls: Confirming Intellectual Disability eligibility mechanically because the English FSIQ of 68 and teacher adaptive score of 71 fall near two standard deviations below the mean.
Dismissing parent-reported home and neighborhood competence as biased while treating a single classroom checklist as definitive adaptive truth.
Postponing all classroom reading and visual accommodations until a full re-evaluation is finalized.
Using an English verbal cognitive subtest with informal on-the-spot translation instead of validated nonverbal or home-language assessment methods.
sampleOutline: Evidence critique: An English IQ of 68 and a single teacher adaptive rating of 71 are invalidated by WIDA Level 2 status, interrupted schooling, uncorrected myopia, and discrepant real-world home-community competence.

AAIDD and IDEA rules: AAIDD requires convergent limitations in intellectual and adaptive functioning interpreted within cultural-linguistic peers and community environments; IDEA bars eligibility driven by limited English proficiency or lack of instruction.

Next-step plan: Coordinate corrective lenses, complete bilingual and nonverbal multidisciplinary evaluation sampling conceptual, social, and practical domains across home and school, and deliver explicit visual-scaffolded reading and ELD instruction.

Safeguards: Maintain interpreter-supported family partnership, analyze instructional response data, and base any future supports plan on verified individual support intensity rather than a flawed label.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Apply legal criteria to an Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS) recommendation
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate an administrator's push to assign a fifth grader with moderate intellectual disability to the Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS) and build an ecological access assessment plan.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Elena, an 11-year-old fifth grader with moderate intellectual disability, decodes CVC and sight words, solves two-step money tasks with a calculator and anchor chart, and joins science labs with graphic organizers. Before state testing, an administrator urges the Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS) because her benchmarks lag two years and she spends 60 percent of her day in resource. Parents got a pre-checked form five minutes early.
taskParts: Evaluate the administrator's rationale and the pre-checked parent form against IDEA and ESSA Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS) eligibility and procedural safeguards.
Design an ecological discrepancy inventory across Elena's fifth-grade general-education literacy, math, and science settings to identify required accommodations and supports.
Specify how the IEP team should document assessment participation, inform parents of long-term diploma implications, and align daily instruction with testing accommodations.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Highlight Elena's active decoding, calculator-assisted two-step math problem solving, and inclusive science lab engagement against the invalid placement-percentage and low-score rationales.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B assessment participation rules (34 CFR 300.160 and 300.320(a)(6)): AA-AAS is strictly for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities, never based on label, setting, or predicted scores, and requires non-predetermined IEP team decision making.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Conduct ecological task-environment analysis across fifth-grade classes, match state-allowed general-assessment accommodations (text-to-speech, extended time, calculation tools where permitted), and embed those exact supports in daily instruction.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Provide written explanation of how AA-AAS participation can affect standard high school diploma pathways, give parents advance review time without pre-checked forms, and review accommodation effectiveness on classroom benchmarks.

successCriteria: Explains that AA-AAS participation is restricted to students with the most significant cognitive disabilities and cannot be triggered by resource-room minutes or below-grade benchmark scores.
Identifies handing parents a pre-checked decision form five minutes prior to the meeting as unlawful predetermination violating meaningful parent participation.
Uses ecological assessment to align daily classroom accommodations with state-permitted general-assessment accommodations rather than lowering curricular expectations.
Requires explicit parent notification regarding potential state diploma and postsecondary impacts whenever alternate standards are considered.
commonPitfalls: Assuming every student eligible under the Intellectual Disability category automatically belongs on the Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS).
Allowing school accountability pressures or predicted proficiency scores to guide an individual student's assessment pathway.
Introducing accommodations for the first time on state testing day without verifying Elena uses them fluently during daily instruction.
Failing to distinguish accommodations that maintain grade-level construct validity from modifications that alter grade-level achievement standards.
sampleOutline: Compliance analysis: Neither Elena's ID label, her 60 percent resource schedule, nor below-grade benchmarks justify AA-AAS; presenting a pre-checked form five minutes before the meeting violates IDEA's prohibition on predetermination.

Ecological assessment: Inventory environmental demands and access barriers in fifth-grade ELA, math, and science to test whether Elena can access the general assessment using allowable accommodations such as read-aloud, visual checklists, and permitted math tools.

IEP team action: Reconvene with advance parent materials, review state AA-AAS eligibility guidelines transparently including diploma-track consequences, and retain Elena on the general grade-level assessment with daily-practiced accommodations if she does not meet most-significant-cognitive-disability criteria.
Monitoring: Track Elena's performance with and without each accommodation across quarterly curriculum-based probes to validate access and inform ongoing instruction.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Eliminate paraprofessional prompt dependence using constant time delay
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a systematic task-analysis, chaining, and prompt-fading protocol to build independent execution of a multi-step school job routine and retrain paraprofessional support.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Tariq, a 14-year-old eighth grader with moderate intellectual disability, is learning an eight-step cafeteria tray-prep and checkout routine. Three-day baseline probes show he independently completes Step 1 (apron) and Step 8 (wipe counter) on 100 percent of trials, but stalls on Steps 2 through 7 waiting for elbow touches or verbal narration. To keep the line moving, his paraprofessional now uses continuous hand-over-hand guidance on every step.
taskParts: Select an appropriate chaining procedure and response-prompting system (Constant Time Delay or System of Least Prompts) justified by Tariq's baseline profile and frustration with errors.
Specify exact 0-second and 4-second delay procedures, controlling prompt, error-correction rule, and transfer of stimulus control to natural environmental cues.
Outline paraprofessional coaching, fidelity checks, and multiple-opportunity probe data graphing to fade adult prompts systematically.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Use baseline mastery of Steps 1 and 8, passive stalling at Steps 2–7, error frustration, and continuous hand-over-hand rushing to pinpoint adult-created prompt dependence.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply evidence-based systematic instruction for ID: total-task chaining, Constant Time Delay (near-errorless acquisition), stimulus-control transfer, and educator supervision of paraprofessionals.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Run total-task chaining with a picture-sequence strip at eye level; teach Steps 2–7 via Constant Time Delay (0-second controlling model prompt shifting to 4-second wait), reinforcing unprompted correct steps immediately.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Score each step as unprompted correct, prompted correct, or error on daily task-analytic probes, conduct weekly paraprofessional procedural-fidelity checks, and schedule practice during lower-rush prep windows first.

successCriteria: Diagnoses prompt dependence caused by continuous hand-over-hand guidance and rapid verbal narration during lunch rush.
Justifies total-task chaining paired with Constant Time Delay (0-second then 4-second delay) to minimize error frustration while preserving mastered Steps 1 and 8.
Defines explicit transfer of stimulus control from the controlling prompt to natural cues and an age-appropriate visual task checklist.
Establishes teacher-led paraprofessional training, procedural-fidelity monitoring, and separate tracking of unprompted versus prompted step mastery.
commonPitfalls: Continuing full hand-over-hand physical prompting across already-mastered Steps 1 and 8 just to speed up cafeteria throughput.
Combining repeated verbal chatter with elbow taps simultaneously so Tariq never learns which natural environmental cue signals the next step.
Graphing combined prompted-plus-independent accuracy, which hides persistent prompt dependence behind artificially high percentages.
Delegating instructional design or prompt-fading decisions solely to the paraprofessional without teacher modeling and fidelity observation.
sampleOutline: Baseline diagnosis: Tariq already performs Steps 1 and 8 independently; stalling on Steps 2–7 reflects prompt dependence reinforced by continuous hand-over-hand rushing.

Systematic instruction design: Use total-task chaining during a low-rush pre-lunch window with Constant Time Delay—two sessions at 0-second delay using a concise model/gesture controlling prompt, then 4-second delay so Tariq anticipates steps from natural cues and a laminated picture strip.
Reinforcement and error correction: Deliver immediate specific praise for unprompted steps and use a calm non-punitive model correction if an error occurs before 4 seconds.

Supervision and data: Train the paraprofessional through modeling and role-play, verify fidelity weekly, and graph independent percentage of steps mastered until Tariq reaches criterion and generalizes to peak lunch service.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Integrate grade-aligned shared reading and SETT-based AAC in 6th-grade ELA
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Replace isolated alphabet worksheets for a sixth grader with intellectual disability and complex communication needs using shared story reading, phonics, and the SETT AAC framework.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Maya, a 12-year-old sixth grader with intellectual disability and complex communication needs, speaks 15 words and points to food photos at lunch. In inclusive sixth-grade ELA, she sits at a back table coloring alphabet sheets while peers study an ecosystem novel. Staff insist Maya must master all 26 letter sounds before joining discussions or trialing a speech-generating device. She loves wildlife videos and laughs at peer jokes in advisory.
taskParts: Refute the letter-sound prerequisite barrier using IDEA LRE access standards and evidence-based comprehensive literacy and AAC principles.
Apply all four components of the SETT framework (Student, Environments, Tasks, Tools) to select and implement a robust core-plus-fringe AAC system across Maya's sixth-grade day.
Design an age-respectful inclusive ELA plan combining adapted grade-aligned shared story reading with systematic foundational decoding instruction.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast Maya's 15 spoken words, food-only photo board, and back-table coloring sheets against her wildlife interests, peer social engagement, and sixth-grade ecosystem unit.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B general-curriculum access (34 CFR 300.320) and assistive technology consideration (34 CFR 300.324(a)(2)(v)); reject prerequisite readiness myths for both AAC and grade-level literature.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Complete a team SETT evaluation to trial a dynamic core-plus-ecosystem-fringe AAC display; seat Maya with table peers for adapted chapter text, repeated story lines, partner-assisted commenting, and separate explicit decoding instruction.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Monitor literal and inferential comprehension responses via AAC, track core-word combinations across ELA and advisory, and ensure every adapted material looks age-respectful for a 12-year-old.

successCriteria: Explicitly dismantles the misconception that mastering all 26 letter sounds is a prerequisite for AAC access or inclusive literature participation.
Systematically walks through Student, Environments, Tasks, and Tools (SETT) before selecting an AAC tool rather than starting with a device catalog.
Pairs age-respectful adapted grade-aligned shared story reading (repeated story line, graphic organizer, core-word commenting) with explicit foundational literacy instruction.
Moves Maya from an isolated back table into authentic peer-group discussions using peer-modeled AAC communication.
commonPitfalls: Replacing grade-level ELA entirely with functional survival sight words or continuing preschool-style coloring worksheets for a 12-year-old.
Limiting Maya's AAC board to choice-making and lunch food nouns rather than generative core vocabulary for commenting, questioning, and peer humor.
Skipping Student, Environment, and Task analysis and jumping straight to purchasing whichever tablet app the district already owns.
Assuming shared story reading alone replaces systematic phonics and phonemic awareness instruction instead of providing comprehensive literacy.
sampleOutline: Barrier analysis: Withholding AAC and peer literature access until Maya masters 26 letter sounds violates IDEA general-curriculum and AT mandates and replaces age-appropriate learning with stigmatizing busywork.

SETT AAC plan: Analyze Student strengths (wildlife interest, peer humor), Environments (6th-grade ELA, science, lunch, advisory), and Tasks (answering text questions, joking with peers, requesting) to trial a robust core-plus-fringe speech-generating system.

Comprehensive literacy design: Seat Maya with peers for shared reading of an adapted ecosystem novel featuring simplified text, visual concept webs, a repeated main-idea line, and AAC-supported WH-comprehension prompts, complemented by brief daily explicit decoding lessons.
Monitoring: Graph independent AAC comprehension turns, communicative functions beyond requesting, and decoding mastery weekly while training ELA teachers and peers in aided language modeling.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Program community generalization and peer supports beyond classroom simulations
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Explain why classroom play-money accuracy failed to transfer to a neighborhood pharmacy and design a generalization-focused Community-Based Instruction and peer-support plan.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Jordan, a 16-year-old tenth grader with moderate intellectual disability, uses the next-dollar strategy with plastic coins in a self-contained classroom store at 95 percent accuracy. On a neighborhood pharmacy trip, Jordan froze at the self-checkout screen, handed a 20-dollar bill for a 3.49-dollar item, and waited while an aide finished paying. In hallways and elective art, Jordan sits beside a 1:1 aide with zero reciprocal peer talks all week.
taskParts: Diagnose the failure to generalize from classroom play money to the pharmacy checkout using evidence-based generalization principles.
Design a structured Community-Based Instruction (CBI) sequence that programs generalization across real currency, varied registers, and authentic community settings.
Replace hovering 1:1 paraprofessional proximity in elective art and hallways with a structured peer-support arrangement that builds natural social belonging.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast 95 percent plastic-coin accuracy against freezing at the pharmacy self-checkout and link zero reciprocal peer talks to continuous 1:1 paraprofessional hovering in art and hallways.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply Stokes and Baer generalization tactics (sufficient exemplars, common stimuli, natural contingencies, teach loosely), CBI aligned with IEP goals, and peer-support arrangements promoting LRE inclusion.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Replace plastic coins with real bills, debit-tap practice, and varied store-kiosk simulations before weekly small-group CBI across multiple stores; coach two art-class peers to share materials and cue transitions while fading aide distance.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Collect generalization probes across untrained stores and items, track reciprocal peer exchanges alongside adult-proximity distance, and ensure CBI respects teen dignity, consent, and community safety.

successCriteria: Identifies artificial classroom stimuli (plastic coins, predictable script) and adult takeover as the root causes of failed community transfer.
Applies explicit generalization programming—real currency, multiple store exemplars, self-checkout screens, and faded prompts—within structured CBI.
Designs an evidence-based peer-support arrangement in tenth-grade art that equips classmates with natural interaction strategies while fading 1:1 adult hovering.
Protects student dignity by scheduling small-group natural community trips and monitoring both independent purchase accuracy and peer-interaction data.
commonPitfalls: Responding to the pharmacy freeze by drilling additional weeks of plastic-coin worksheets inside the self-contained classroom.
Allowing the aide to step in and finish checkout transactions quickly, inadvertently reinforcing passivity and learned helplessness.
Running large, conspicuous group CBI trips where teenagers wear matching school lanyards that single them out and block natural community interaction.
Assigning classmates as unpaid mini-teachers or charity helpers rather than reciprocal peers sharing an authentic art activity.
sampleOutline: Generalization diagnosis: Classroom plastic coins lacked common stimuli with real bills and touch-screen self-checkouts, and immediate aide takeover blocked independent problem solving.

CBI generalization plan: Program common stimuli and sufficient exemplars by practicing next-dollar and card-tap purchases with real money across varied prices, followed by weekly small-group CBI at two to three local stores with systematic prompt fading.

Peer-support arrangement: In tenth-grade art, partner Jordan with two trained peers who share supplies and model studio routines while the paraprofessional fades to periodic check-ins across the room.
Safeguards and data: Secure parent permission and safety protocols for CBI, graph independent steps at untrained stores, and track weekly reciprocal peer exchanges versus adult proximity.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Rebuild a transition IEP around student voice, SDM, and integrated work
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Audit a noncompliant secondary transition IEP for a 17-year-old with intellectual disability and redesign it around self-determination, Supported Decision-Making, and competitive integrated employment.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Sofia, a 17-year-old junior with intellectual disability, enjoys arranging floral displays and greeting shoppers at a local garden center. Yet her draft IEP repeats last year's sheltered-workshop packet goal, and staff excluded her from the last meeting believing it would confuse her. Approaching age 18, a caseworker told her parents they must obtain plenary guardianship to keep signing forms, and Vocational Rehabilitation was not invited.
taskParts: Identify IDEA Part B secondary transition violations in Sofia's excluded attendance, recycled sheltered-workshop goal, and omitted Vocational Rehabilitation invitation.
Clarify transfer-of-rights rules at the age of majority and compare full plenary guardianship with less-restrictive Supported Decision-Making (SDM) options.
Design a person-centered transition plan featuring student-led IEP preparation, age-appropriate transition assessments, and competitive supported employment with fading job coaching.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast Sofia's genuine garden-center strengths and approaching 18th birthday against her exclusion from IEP meetings, recycled sheltered-workshop goal, absent VR representative, and blanket guardianship advice.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B transition rules (34 CFR 300.320(b)-(c), 300.321(b)): mandatory student invitation, age-appropriate transition assessments, measurable postsecondary goals, consent-based VR invitation, and one-year-prior transfer-of-rights notice.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Prepare Sofia with visual slides to co-lead her IEP, obtain consent to invite VR for competitive supported employment and job carving at a retail nursery, and share objective state-specific resources on Supported Decision-Making and limited powers of attorney.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Verify current state law on age of majority and SDM agreements without offering legal representation, track natural coworker supports as job coaching fades, and update postsecondary goals annually from situational work assessments.

successCriteria: Cites IDEA requirements to invite Sofia to every transition IEP meeting, update measurable postsecondary goals from current transition assessments, and seek consent to invite Vocational Rehabilitation.
Replaces segregated sheltered-workshop defaults with competitive integrated employment options such as job carving, situational assessment, and fading job-coach supports.
Accurately explains age-of-majority transfer-of-rights notice (at least one year before age 18) and presents Supported Decision-Making as a less-restrictive alternative to plenary guardianship.
Includes concrete self-determination scaffolds (choice making, visual meeting script, goal-setting practice) so Sofia actively leads her transition planning.
commonPitfalls: Endorsing the caseworker's claim that plenary guardianship is automatically required at age 18 for every student with an intellectual disability.
Inviting Vocational Rehabilitation to the IEP meeting without first securing written consent from Sofia's parents (or from Sofia once rights transfer).
Copying prior-year transition goals verbatim or equating a student's disability label with sheltered-workshop placement.
Inviting Sofia to sit silently in the IEP meeting without pre-teaching accessible self-advocacy tools so she can participate meaningfully.
sampleOutline: IDEA audit: Excluding Sofia violates 34 CFR 300.321(b), copying a sheltered-workshop goal ignores current assessment of her garden-center strengths, and failing to seek consent to invite VR weakens interagency transition linkages.

Transfer of rights and SDM: IDEA requires notifying Sofia and her parents at least one year before the age of majority; educators should provide unbiased information on less-restrictive options such as Supported Decision-Making agreements or educational proxies rather than pushing plenary guardianship, directing legal questions to qualified state resources.

Person-centered transition plan: Conduct situational vocational assessment at a local nursery, coach Sofia to present her strengths and goals using a visual slide deck at her IEP, and partner with VR (with prior consent) on customized supported employment and fading job coaching.
Monitoring: Track Sofia's workplace task mastery, natural coworker supports, and self-advocacy milestones quarterly across her senior year.
