quickReference.domainLabel: Development and Characteristics of Students with Intellectual Disabilities
quickReference.title: AAIDD Three-Prong Criteria, Etiologies & Supports Paradigm
quickReference.purpose: Anchors AAIDD and IDEA intellectual disability definitions, adaptive behavior domains, genetic syndrome precautions, and supports-intensity classification.
checklist: Confirm concurrent significant limitations in both intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior plus developmental-period onset before concluding Intellectual Disability.
Evaluate coexisting sensory, speech-language, motor, cardiac, seizure, or orthopedic health needs associated with specific genetic or environmental etiologies.
Frame learner profiles around the AAIDD supports paradigm (what intensity of supports enables participation) rather than static IQ ceilings.
formulas: AAIDD (12th ed.) and IDEA three-prong ID criteria: (1) significant limitations in intellectual functioning (~2 SD below mean, IQ ~70 plus/minus 5 SEM), (2) significant limitations in adaptive behavior (~2 SD below mean in conceptual, social, OR practical domain, or overall score), and (3) onset during the developmental period (AAIDD age 22; IDEA age 18/developmental period).

AAIDD three adaptive behavior domains: Conceptual (language, reading/writing, money, time, number concepts), Social (interpersonal skills, social responsibility, self-esteem, gullibility/naivete, rule following), and Practical (daily living, occupational skills, healthcare, travel, safety, schedules).

AAIDD Supports Intensity levels (replacing fixed IQ-only labels): Intermittent (as-needed episodic), Limited (time-limited consistent, such as job-start coaching), Extensive (regular daily involvement in at least some environments), and Pervasive (constant high-intensity life-sustaining supports across environments).

High-yield syndrome medical and learning profiles: Down syndrome/Trisomy 21 (check atlantoaxial instability before tumbling/contact sports, conductive hearing loss, congenital heart defects, visual-processing strengths vs expressive language delays); Fragile X (hyperarousal, gaze aversion, sensory sensitivities); Prader-Willi (hyperphagia/food-safety routines, hypotonia); Williams (strong sociability/auditory memory vs visuospatial/math delays); FASD (executive-function and working-memory deficits).
decisionRules: When a student scores IQ 67 on a cognitive battery but demonstrates age-appropriate conceptual, social, and practical adaptive skills across home and school → prioritize NOT identifying Intellectual Disability, because both intellectual and adaptive limitations must coexist.

When a student with Down syndrome is cleared for adaptive PE and floor gymnastics → prioritize checking medical clearance for atlantoaxial instability (cervical spine) and leveraging visual modeling alongside spoken directions.

When a student with Prader-Willi syndrome attends school cafeteria and cooking labs → prioritize structured environmental food-security routines, predictable schedules, and nurse/family health coordination.

When a student with Intellectual Disability struggles to transfer classroom skills to community settings → prioritize teaching with concrete real-world materials, explicit generalization cues, and distributed practice to counter working-memory and transfer limits.
cautions: Never determine Intellectual Disability from an IQ score alone without standardized adaptive behavior evidence across settings and cultural-linguistic consideration.
Do not interpret gullibility, literal language processing, or slow response latency as willful noncompliance.
Avoid attributing all learning or behavioral struggles to the ID label (diagnostic overshadowing) without checking for treatable vision, hearing, pain, or mental-health comorbidities.

quickReference.domainLabel: Planning and Managing the Learning Environment
quickReference.title: Person-Centered IEPs, Self-Determination, Transition & AAC
quickReference.purpose: Anchors person-centered planning, Wehmeyer self-determination components, IDEA secondary transition mandates, SETT assistive technology, and positive inclusive routines.
checklist: Center the student’s own preferences, strengths, communication system, and post-school vision in every IEP and transition planning meeting.
Balance grade-aligned academic access with chronological-age-appropriate functional life and community skills in inclusive settings.
Verify that AAC devices, visual schedules, and environmental supports travel seamlessly across classrooms, lunch, community sites, and home.
formulas: Person-Centered Planning tools: MAPS (Making Action Plans), PATH (Planning Alternative Tomorrows with Hope), and Essential Lifestyle Planning place the student and chosen allies at the center to build strengths-based community and post-school visions.

Wehmeyer Self-Determination instructional components: choice-making, decision-making, problem-solving, goal-setting and attainment, self-regulation/self-management, self-advocacy, internal locus of control, and self-awareness (taught explicitly through frameworks such as the Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction, SDLMI).

IDEA secondary transition and adult-life benchmarks (34 CFR 300.320 & 300.305): transition IEP by age 16 with measurable postsecondary goals (education/training, employment, independent living), interagency links (Vocational Rehabilitation / WIOA Pre-ETS, customized/supported employment), age-of-majority notice 1 year before legal adulthood, and a Summary of Performance (SOP) upon graduation or aging out.

SETT framework for AT/AAC and positive routines: match Student abilities, Environments, and Tasks before selecting Tools (low-tech PECS/communication boards to high-tech SGD with core vocabulary); embed peer-mediated supports and proactive PBIS routines to prevent prompt dependence.
decisionRules: When a 16-year-old with moderate ID has never participated in their own IEP meeting → prioritize preparing the student using a person-centered visual presentation or AAC script to share strengths, interests, and postsecondary goals during the meeting.

When a team wants to purchase an expensive high-tech tablet app before evaluating classroom routines → prioritize running a SETT analysis (Student, Environments, Tasks, Tools) with the SLP and trialing candidate AAC systems in real routines first.

When an 18-year-old student with ID prepares to exit school into competitive integrated employment → prioritize coordinating WIOA Vocational Rehabilitation Pre-ETS, natural workplace job coaching, community mobility training, and a detailed Summary of Performance.

When a paraprofessional hovers directly beside a student with ID in general education and answers peer questions on the student’s behalf → prioritize fading adult proximity and training natural peer supports to foster belonging and independence.
cautions: Never use preschool cartoons, babyish worksheets, or developmentally patronizing materials with adolescents with Intellectual Disability; maintain chronological age appropriateness.
Do not lock a student’s AAC device away during recess, lunch, or field trips or withhold communication access as a behavioral consequence.
Avoid treating sheltered workshops or non-integrated day programs as the default post-school track when competitive integrated or supported employment is feasible with job coaching.

quickReference.title: Systematic Instruction, Chaining, Functional Literacy & Math
quickReference.purpose: Anchors response-prompting hierarchies, task-analysis chaining, integrated functional-academic literacy, functional mathematics, and community generalization.
checklist: Determine whether the target skill is discrete (single response like reading a word) or chained (multi-step sequence like purchasing groceries) before choosing time delay versus chaining.
Select an error-minimizing prompting procedure with an explicit plan to transfer stimulus control from teacher prompts to natural environmental cues.
Combine functional life-skills instruction with meaningful grade-aligned literacy, communication, and numeracy instruction.
formulas: Response-prompting procedures: Constant Time Delay (CTD: 0-second simultaneous controlling prompt during initial acquisition, then fixed 3 to 5 second wait to transfer stimulus control); Progressive Time Delay (PTD: gradually lengthen delay 0s, 1s, 2s, 4s); System of Least Prompts (SLP: independent → verbal/gesture → model → physical, moving up only as needed); Most-to-Least (MTL: begin with full prompt and systematically fade for safety-critical or error-sensitive tasks).

Task analysis and chaining: break complex routines into observable sequential steps; Forward Chaining teaches step 1 first (teacher completes remainder); Backward Chaining teacher completes early steps and student performs final step for immediate natural reinforcement; Total-Task Chaining teaches every step each trial with just-enough prompting (best when student already knows several steps).

Balanced literacy for ID: combine systematic phonics/decoding and phonemic awareness (Early Reading Skills Builder / adapted structured literacy) with functional sight words (safety/community words), shared story reading with adapted grade-level texts, and core-vocabulary AAC writing.

Functional math and generalization: Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA), Next-Dollar (Dollar-Up) strategy for real-currency purchasing, tactile/digital clocks for schedule management, Community-Based Instruction (CBI) in authentic venues, and General Case Instruction sampling the full range of real-world stimulus variations.
decisionRules: When introducing a new safety sign or sight-word set to a student who makes frequent impulsive guesses → prioritize 0-second Constant Time Delay for initial errorless rounds, then shift to a 4-second delay so the student responds independently before the controlling prompt.

When teaching a student with moderate ID to wash hands or tie shoes who gets frustrated before reaching the end → prioritize Backward Chaining so the student completes the final step and immediately experiences natural completion reinforcement.

When a student can count plastic coins accurately in a worksheet workbook but cannot pay for a $3.45 cafeteria meal → prioritize Community-Based Instruction using real bills and the Next-Dollar strategy across multiple store cashiers (General Case Instruction).

When a student already performs 6 of 10 steps of a microwave-snack task analysis independently → prioritize Total-Task Chaining with System of Least Prompts on only the 4 unmastered steps rather than restarting from step 1.
cautions: Never use only functional sight-word memorization while denying students with Intellectual Disability access to explicit phonemic awareness, decoding, and adapted grade-level literature.
Do not deliver prompts inconsistently or jump in after 1 second when a student needs 4 to 5 seconds of processing wait time, which cements prompt dependency.
Avoid teaching community skills solely through classroom simulations without scheduled in-vivo practice in authentic grocery, transit, or workplace settings.

quickReference.title: Adaptive Scales, Ecological Inventories & ESSA 1% AA-AAS Rules
quickReference.purpose: Anchors adaptive-behavior assessment instruments, ecological discrepancy inventories, ESSA 1% alternate-assessment rules, and systematic prompt-level progress monitoring.
checklist: Verify that adaptive behavior is assessed with standardized informants across both home and school environments (such as Vineland-3, ABAS-3, or DABS).
Confirm that Alternate Assessment (AA-AAS) participation reflects the most significant cognitive disabilities rather than convenience, attendance, or an ID label alone.
Track both accuracy and prompt-level independence on task-analysis and discrete-trial graphs to make timely instructional adjustments.
formulas: Standardized adaptive and ecological assessment: Vineland-3, ABAS-3, and Diagnostic Adaptive Behavior Scale (DABS) quantify conceptual, social, and practical functioning; Ecological Inventories map natural environment demands → sub-environments → activities → skills → discrepancy analysis to pinpoint teaching targets or adaptations.

ESSA 1% AA-AAS federal cap (34 CFR 200.6(c)): states may assess no more than 1.0% of total tested students per subject via Alternate Assessments aligned with Alternate Academic Achievement Standards (AA-AAS); reserved exclusively for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities based on IEP team state-guideline decisions (never a district-level individual-student quota prohibiting eligible learners).

Parent notice for AA-AAS (ESSA): IEP teams must inform parents clearly how alternate-achievement participation affects eligibility for a standard high school diploma versus an alternate credential, while preserving grade-level general curriculum access.

Instructional progress monitoring for ID: chart percentage of task-analysis steps performed independently, prompt-level reduction curves (full physical → partial → model → verbal → independent), and FBA-linked replacement-behavior rates to guide systematic prompt fading.
decisionRules: When a principal tells an IEP team to move a student with mild ID onto the Alternate Assessment to raise school proficiency averages → prioritize rejecting the request and evaluating participation strictly against state most-significant-cognitive-disability criteria.

When a standardized cognitive test has a cultural/linguistic mismatch for a multilingual learner suspected of ID → prioritize nonverbal cognitive indices, bilingual assessment, home-language adaptive interviews, and dynamic ecological evidence.

When weekly task-analysis data show a student stays stuck at "verbal prompt" on step 4 for three consecutive weeks → prioritize analyzing the step barrier (task modification, visual cue, or brief backward-chaining focus on step 4) rather than repeating unchanged trials.

When planning community-living IEP goals for a 15-year-old with moderate ID → prioritize conducting an Ecological Inventory and discrepancy analysis across the student’s actual neighborhood, school cafeteria, and transit routes.
cautions: Never assign a student to the AA-AAS automatically just because their IDEA eligibility category is Intellectual Disability; many students with mild ID participate in regular assessments with accommodations.

Do not interpret the federal 1% AA-AAS state cap as an illegal school-level ceiling that bars a legitimately eligible student with the most significant cognitive disabilities from alternate assessment.
Avoid testing a student with ID without ensuring glasses, hearing aids, AAC devices, and familiar response modes are active throughout administration.

quickReference.title: Disability Rights, Supported Decision-Making & Team Supervision
quickReference.purpose: Anchors IDEA, ADA/Olmstead community rights, Supported Decision-Making versus guardianship, CEC ethical dignity standards, and paraprofessional supervision.
checklist: Distinguish IDEA entitlement rights in K-12 schooling from ADA/Section 504 nondiscrimination eligibility protections in adult employment and postsecondary settings.
Verify least-restrictive adult decision-making options (Supported Decision-Making, powers of attorney) before discussing plenary guardianship with families.
Ensure paraprofessionals receive written task directions, modeling, and ongoing supervision while certified teachers retain assessment and planning authority.
formulas: Statutory continuum across the lifespan: IDEA guarantees FAPE in LRE through age 21 or regular diploma; Section 504 (Rehabilitation Act) and ADA Title II/III protect against discrimination and require reasonable accommodations across postsecondary, transit, and employment; Olmstead v. L.C. (1999) affirms the right to live and receive services in the most integrated community setting.

Age of majority and Supported Decision-Making (SDM): IDEA requires written transfer-of-rights notice at least 1 year before legal adulthood (typically 18); SDM lets adults with ID retain legal rights while choosing trusted supporters to help weigh options—always explored as a less-restrictive alternative before guardianship.

Paraprofessional supervision framework (CEC): certified special educator designs curriculum, writes IEP goals, conducts formal evaluations, communicates diagnostic/IEP status to families, and trains/monitors paraprofessionals; paraprofessionals deliver pre-planned instruction, implement behavior/prompt plans faithfully, and record objective data.

Dignity, safety, and advocacy ethics: uphold person-first or individual-preferred identity language, protect bodily privacy during personal-care routines, teach abuse-prevention and consent/boundary skills explicitly, and collaborate seamlessly with SLP, OT, PT, school nurse, and adult VR agencies.
decisionRules: When parents of a 17-year-old with ID assume they must petition for full legal guardianship on their child’s 18th birthday → prioritize sharing objective information on transfer of rights, Supported Decision-Making agreements, limited powers of attorney, and community legal-aid resources.

When a newly hired paraprofessional begins improvising simplified worksheets and altering a student’s prompting hierarchy without teacher input → prioritize providing clear written instructional plans, live coaching, and scheduled feedback check-ins while reinforcing role boundaries.

When a general-education teacher excludes a student with ID from a grade-level science lab field trip citing "safety and pacing" → prioritize advocating for LRE participation in nonacademic/extracurricular activities (34 CFR 300.107) with appropriate supplementary aids and safety supports.
When teaching community independence to young adults with ID → prioritize embedding explicit personal-safety, consent, scam-recognition, and self-advocacy instruction alongside vocational skills.
cautions: Never give legal advice telling parents they must obtain guardianship, or assume that an Intellectual Disability diagnosis automatically negates adult legal capacity.
Do not delegate primary instruction, IEP goal authorship, or formal parent progress conferences solely to a paraprofessional.
Avoid discussing a student’s health, toileting, or behavioral plans in hallways or shared lounges where peers or unauthorized staff can overhear.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Diagnosing Intellectual Disability by IQ Cutoff Alone Instead of the AAIDD Three-Prong Criteria
misconceptionFamilies.description: Treating an IQ score below 70 as sufficient to diagnose Intellectual Disability while overlooking concurrent significant limitations in adaptive behavior (conceptual, social, and practical domains) and developmental-period onset, or grouping students by IQ label instead of the AAIDD intensity-of-supports model.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify all three mandatory AAIDD/IDEA criteria—significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (roughly two standard deviations below the mean with standard error of measurement), concurrent adaptive behavior deficits across conceptual/social/practical skills, and developmental-period onset—and plan services by needed support intensity (intermittent, limited, extensive, pervasive).

misconceptionFamilies.label: Diagnostic Overshadowing That Attributes Medical, Sensory, or Emotional Changes to ID
misconceptionFamilies.description: Dismissing abrupt behavioral changes, fatigue, irritability, self-injury, or skill regression as inherent features of a student's intellectual disability instead of investigating unexpressed physical pain, medication side effects, seizure activity, hearing or vision loss, or co-occurring mental health conditions.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Treat any sudden change in behavior, alertness, or baseline performance as a red flag requiring immediate medical, sensory, medication, and environmental rule-out before attributing it to intellectual disability or designing a behavior-reduction plan.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Mismatching Task Analysis with Forward, Backward, or Total-Task Chaining
misconceptionFamilies.description: Teaching complex multi-step academic or daily-living routines as a single undifferentiated prompt, or defaulting blindly to forward chaining when backward chaining delivers immediate natural reinforcement on the final step or total-task chaining matches a student who already completes scattered steps.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Validate a discrete, observable step-by-step task analysis first, then select backward chaining when immediate natural completion reinforcement motivates a beginner, forward chaining when early steps are easiest to secure, or total-task presentation when the student already performs multiple steps across the sequence.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Creating Prompt Dependence by Failing to Fade Prompts Systematically
misconceptionFamilies.description: Delivering continuous verbal reminders, hovering gestures, or full physical hand-over-hand guidance on every trial without a systematic fading plan, leaving the student waiting for adult prompts instead of responding to natural environmental cues.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Select an evidence-based response-prompting system—constant or progressive time delay (0-second errorless trials → 4-second delay), least-to-most prompting for partially acquired skills, or most-to-least fading for novel/safety-critical steps—and track unprompted independence to transfer stimulus control to natural cues.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Over-Assigning Alternate Assessments (AA-AAS) Based on Disability Label Alone
misconceptionFamilies.description: Automatically assigning every student with an intellectual disability to Alternate Assessments Based on Alternate Academic Achievement Standards (AA-AAS) solely because of their IDEA category or below-grade test scores, without checking eligibility for the most significant cognitive disabilities or disclosing graduation-diploma impacts to parents.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Restrict AA-AAS strictly to the small proportion of students with the most significant cognitive disabilities who require extensive, direct individualized instruction and substantial supports to achieve measurable gains on grade-aligned alternate standards, and always inform parents in writing of diploma implications.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Using Infantile Materials and Neglecting Generalization, CBI, and Postsecondary Transition
misconceptionFamilies.description: Giving adolescents with intellectual disabilities preschool-themed worksheets instead of chronologically age-appropriate materials, rehearsing life skills only in artificial classroom simulations without Community-Based Instruction (CBI), or writing compliance-only transition plans without student self-determination and adult-agency linkages.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Use chronologically age-appropriate materials aligned to functional and grade-level standards, teach directly in authentic community settings using multiple exemplars to secure generalization, and build student-led postsecondary transition plans (by age 16 under IDEA, or younger per state rule) backed by age-appropriate transition assessments and agency linkages.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Diagnosing Intellectual Disability by IQ Cutoff Alone Instead of the AAIDD Three-Prong Criteria
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Verify All Three AAIDD Diagnostic Prongs and Plan by Intensity of Supports
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A 5322 case presents a student with an IQ score of 68 who demonstrates strong everyday adaptive skills (or a student with an IQ of 72 whose SEM band overlaps 70 alongside major adaptive deficits) and tempts you to decide eligibility from the IQ number alone.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are all three prongs satisfied—intellectual functioning (interpreting SEM), concurrent conceptual/social/practical adaptive limitations, and developmental-period onset—and are services planned by individualized support intensity rather than IQ tier?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check the case data for all three required diagnostic components (IQ with confidence band, standardized adaptive behavior scores across conceptual/social/practical domains, and onset before age 22 under AAIDD 12th ed. or age 18 in legacy state rules) and spot any distractor that treats IQ as a rigid standalone cutoff.
stages.requiredOutput: Audit which of the three prongs are met or missing in the vignette and flag any rigid-IQ-cutoff or label-driven placement distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Map the three adaptive behavior domains (Conceptual: literacy, money, time; Social: interpersonal skills, gullibility, rule-following; Practical: daily living, health care, travel, occupational skills) and pair them with the four AAIDD support-intensity levels (Intermittent, Limited, Extensive, Pervasive).
stages.requiredOutput: Write one school example for each adaptive domain and explain why two students with identical IQ scores can require totally different support intensities.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Evaluate two referral profiles: Student A has a Full Scale IQ of 69 but age-appropriate adaptive functioning across home, school, and peer settings; Student B has an IQ of 73 (SEM +/- 4), significant deficits in practical and conceptual adaptive scales, and documented early developmental delays.
stages.requiredOutput: Explain why Student A does NOT meet ID criteria (missing concurrent adaptive deficit) while Student B warrants full multidisciplinary review considering SEM and adaptive limitations.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh 5322 item asking how an IEP team should classify and organize instructional supports for a newly identified middle schooler with Down syndrome.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose individualized support-intensity planning across environments rather than assigning a blanket classroom based on mild/moderate/severe IQ bands.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Diagnostic Overshadowing That Attributes Medical, Sensory, or Emotional Changes to ID
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Rule Out Medical, Sensory, and Mental Health Causes Before Attributing Changes to ID
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A student with an intellectual disability who is normally cheerful suddenly hits their ear, refuses lunch, falls asleep in class, or shows sharp skill regression—and distractors assume it is "typical ID behavior" or jump straight to punitive consequences.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Could this sudden change in behavior, alertness, or performance be signaling untreated pain, medication side effects, seizures, sensory loss, or a co-occurring psychiatric condition masked by diagnostic overshadowing?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot abrupt baseline shifts (sudden aggression, ear-hitting, lethargy, withdrawal, loss of previously mastered skills) and recognize diagnostic overshadowing whenever a distractor blames the student's intellectual disability without investigating physical or mental health causes.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the baseline shift in the vignette and identify the diagnostic-overshadowing error in the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the four-domain rule-out protocol for sudden behavioral or cognitive change in students with ID: (1) acute pain/illness (dental, ear infection, GI distress), (2) medication changes or side effects (sedation, irritability), (3) neurological/sensory shifts (absence seizures, progressive hearing/vision loss common in syndromes such as Down or Fragile X), and (4) co-occurring emotional/psychiatric distress (anxiety, depression, trauma).
stages.requiredOutput: List the immediate team communication sequence (school nurse, family consultation, medical/audiological/vision referral) prior to revising a behavior plan.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A nonverbal tenth grader with moderate ID suddenly starts slapping his jaw, refusing preferred snacks, and pushing away staff during morning math. Contrast a diagnostic-overshadowing reaction with an evidence-based response.
stages.requiredOutput: Prioritize immediate school-nurse screening and parent contact to evaluate dental pain or ear infection rather than assuming task-escape defiance or writing a punishment contingency.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5322 vignette describing a student with Down syndrome whose reading participation drops steadily over two months alongside turning one ear toward the speaker.
stages.requiredOutput: Select immediate audiological and vision screening collaboration with the family and nurse before attributing declining performance to cognitive plateau.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Mismatching Task Analysis with Forward, Backward, or Total-Task Chaining
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Match Validated Task Analyses to Forward, Backward, or Total-Task Chaining
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An instructional item asks how to teach a multi-step routine—such as making a microwave lunch, washing hands, using a debit card, or solving a multi-step math routine—and distractors pick the wrong chaining direction for the learner's profile.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which steps of the validated task analysis can the student already perform, and will immediate natural completion reinforcement (backward), early-step momentum (forward), or full-sequence prompting (total-task) yield the fastest mastery?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check the student's single-opportunity or multiple-opportunity baseline probe across the task analysis to see whether they know zero steps, need quick contact with the finished product, or already perform several scattered steps.
stages.requiredOutput: State the learner's baseline pattern across the task steps and flag any distractor that teaches the entire complex routine unsegmented or picks a mismatched chaining direction.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Differentiate the three chaining strategies: Forward Chaining (teach step 1 to mastery, adult completes remaining steps; strong when initial steps are simple and build momentum), Backward Chaining (adult completes all steps except the final step so the learner immediately accesses the natural terminal reinforcer—such as eating the snack or wearing the zipped jacket), and Total-Task Chaining (learner attempts every step in sequence on each trial with individualized prompts only on unmastered steps; best when the student already knows several steps).
stages.requiredOutput: Write a 3-row selection rule pairing Forward, Backward, and Total-Task Chaining with their ideal learner baseline and reinforcement advantage.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Match two students to the best chaining procedure: (a) a student who gets frustrated quickly and gives up when learning to brew hot cocoa from a 9-step sequence, and (b) a student who already completes 6 of 10 steps of setting a cafeteria workstation independently.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign backward chaining to student (a) so they immediately finish and drink the cocoa after mastering step 9, and total-task chaining to student (b) with targeted prompts only on the 4 missing steps.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a fresh 5322 vignette asking how to verify whether a drafted task analysis for using a laundromat washer is ready for instruction.
stages.requiredOutput: Select performing or observing a competent peer execute the steps in the actual setting and collecting a baseline probe to validate step granularity before teaching.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Creating Prompt Dependence by Failing to Fade Prompts Systematically
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Transfer Stimulus Control to Natural Cues Through Systematic Prompt Fading
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A student with an intellectual disability sits passively until a paraprofessional taps the desk, repeats "What's next?", or guides their hand—showing prompt dependence rather than genuine skill deficit.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What natural environmental cue should trigger this behavior, and which exact systematic prompt-fading protocol (time delay, least-to-most, or most-to-least) will shift control off the adult and onto that natural cue?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the vignette for prompt-dependence signs (the student waits for eye contact, verbal cues, or physical touch before acting) and remember that verbal prompts are often the hardest to fade.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the artificial adult prompt currently controlling the behavior and name the natural stimulus cue that should replace it.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Sequence the prompt hierarchy from least to most intrusive (Natural Cue → Indirect Verbal/Gesture → Visual/Model → Direct Verbal → Partial Physical → Full Physical) and match three fading protocols: Constant Time Delay (0-second errorless trials followed by fixed 4-second delay before the controlling prompt), Least-to-Most (give the learner a chance to respond at each level before increasing assistance), and Most-to-Least (begin with full errorless support for new/safety-critical skills and systematically drop down the hierarchy).
stages.requiredOutput: Explain how 0-second to 4-second constant time delay prevents errors early while giving the learner space to beat the prompt and earn stronger reinforcement for unprompted responses.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A seventh grader with ID reads sight words accurately whenever the paraprofessional points and gives the first sound, but freezes silently when looking at a cafeteria menu alone. Build a prompt-fading plan.
stages.requiredOutput: Replace continuous verbal/pointing cues with constant time delay (0-second model trials → 4-second wait), reinforce unprompted responses differentially, and fade adult proximity using a visual checklist.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a new 5322 instructional-environment item asking how a teacher should coach a paraprofessional who habitually completes zippering and locker opening for a student.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose training the paraprofessional to pause 4 to 5 seconds after the natural cue, use the least intrusive prompt needed, and step back physically as soon as the student initiates.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Over-Assigning Alternate Assessments (AA-AAS) Based on Disability Label Alone
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Apply Strict AA-AAS Participation Criteria and Protect General-Curriculum Access
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An assessment item suggests moving a student with mild intellectual disability onto the state Alternate Assessment Based on Alternate Academic Achievement Standards (AA-AAS) simply because they read two grades below peers or carry an ID eligibility label.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this student truly have the most significant cognitive disability requiring extensive direct individualized instruction on grade-aligned alternate standards—and have parents been informed of diploma consequences?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check the vignette for improper AA-AAS rationales (disability category alone, expected low score on general assessment, English-learner status, poor attendance, or behavioral challenges) versus genuine participation criteria.
stages.requiredOutput: Flag the unlawful or over-broad rationale for AA-AAS placement in the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Lock in the federal ESSA/IDEA AA-AAS guardrails: (1) IEP team decision guided by state participation guidelines (not disability label), (2) reserved for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities (contextualized by ESSA's 1% state participation cap, though never a hard individual quota), (3) aligned to grade-level academic content standards with reduced depth/breadth/complexity (not separate pre-K content), and (4) mandatory parent notification about how AA-AAS affects regular high school diploma eligibility.
stages.requiredOutput: List three factors that can NEVER justify AA-AAS placement and three mandatory elements the IEP team must verify and document when AA-AAS is appropriate.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Decide assessment participation for two fifth graders with ID: Student 1 has mild ID, reads at a third-grade level with text-to-speech, and works on grade-5 content with accommodations; Student 2 has significant cognitive and communication disabilities requiring pervasive supports and individualized grade-5 alternate standards.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign Student 1 to the general state assessment with IEP accommodations and Student 2 to AA-AAS with documented parent notification and grade-5-aligned alternate standards.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5322 accountability item asking what happens if a state approaches the ESSA 1% cap while an IEP team determines a specific student clearly meets all AA-AAS criteria.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the legally accurate principle: the 1% threshold is a state-level accountability cap that NEVER overrides an individual IEP team's data-based participation decision.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Using Infantile Materials and Neglecting Generalization, CBI, and Postsecondary Transition
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Design Age-Appropriate CBI, Generalization Plans, and Student-Led Transition
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A secondary vignette hands a 16-year-old cartoon phonics worksheets, practices grocery checkout solely with plastic classroom coins, or writes a transition plan without the student's voice, age-appropriate assessments, or adult-agency links.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are the materials chronologically respectful, are skills taught in real community settings across multiple exemplars for generalization, and is the student actively driving measurable postsecondary transition goals?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check the student's chronological age against the materials and tasks proposed, and look for simulation-only instruction (no transfer to real community environments) or missing IDEA transition components (postsecondary education/training, employment, independent living where appropriate).
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the age-appropriateness, generalization, or IDEA transition compliance gap in the scenario.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Combine three evidence-based practices for adolescents with ID: (1) Chronological Age-Appropriateness (adapted graphic novels, smartphone budgeting apps, real workplace menus rather than preschool themes), (2) Generalization & CBI (train in real stores/transit/workplaces, use General Case Instruction across varied cashiers/machines/lighting, teach self-management cues), and (3) IDEA Postsecondary Transition (in effect by age 16 or younger per state rule, based on age-appropriate transition assessments, student-led IEP participation, and outside-agency invitations with parent/adult-student consent).
stages.requiredOutput: Specify how General Case Instruction during CBI solves the classroom-simulation transfer failure and name the three required IDEA postsecondary transition domains.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Upgrade a 17-year-old's IEP plan that currently uses kindergarten counting bears for money practice and states a vague transition goal ("will get a job after high school").
stages.requiredOutput: Replace counting bears with real currency/debit-card CBI next-dollar practice across three community stores, and rewrite the transition goal into a measurable employment goal paired with a Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) referral (with consent) and a work-based learning course of study.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh 5322 transition vignette where a student with ID wants to work in an animal shelter, yet staff want to assign her to the school's pre-set cafeteria-cleaning crew.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose honoring student self-determination through situational vocational assessment and community job-sampling aligned to the student's expressed preferences and strengths.
